# Classical Art Museums: Genuine Masterpieces

The fact that some of the works in art museums are several centuries old does not mean that they are just dusty cultural artefacts. On the contrary! Most museums display their treasures to their best advantage, be it in refurbished spaces or via digital media devices.

Almost every visitor to Dresden has the Zwinger on their itinerary. No wonder, since the impressive building complex is one of Germany's most important baroque buildings. Not to mention the interior features! The Old Masters Art Gallery housed here is one of the most renowned collections of paintings in the world. The "Who's Who" of painting, from Peter Paul Rubens to Albrecht Dürer, is gathered across three floors, focusing in particular on the Renaissance period. More than 300 paintings from across the 15th to 18th centuries, including Vermeer's "The Procuress", Correggio's "Nativity", Titian's "Sleeping Venus" and Raphael's "Sistine Madonna" with its two iconic angels, are on display in the gallery's high, light-filled rooms. The collections of pastels by Rosalba Carriera and paintings by Lucas Cranach are also unique. The goal is to linger instead of rushing through. Especially since the museum has really smartened itself up in 2020. In addition to the careful but decisive modernisation of the building, numerous works were restored, and frames freshly gilded or recreated from scratch. Additionally, extensive accent lighting allows paintings and sculptures to appear literally in the best possible light. A special highlight of the newly-designed Semper Gallery is the integration of the renowned so-called Sculpture Collection, with sculptural works spanning five millennia, from Assyrian relief panels to valuable terracottas and vases.

## Städel Museum: 700 Years of Art History Under One Roof

**Frankfurt/Main: Städel Museum** ©#visitfrankfurt (Holger Ullmann)

Frankfurt is not only a financial centre, but also a museum capital. A phenomenal 38 exhibition venues, from the Film Museum to the Architecture Museum to the Jewish Museum, make up the "Museumsufer Frankfurt", an unparalleled cultural hotspot. Right in the middle: the Städel Museum, one of the most important art museums in the country. Founded in 1815 by the banker and merchant Johann Friedrich Städel, the museum collection is the oldest and most renowned in the country. Over the years, it has collected more than 3,100 paintings, 660 sculptures, 5,000 photographs and over 100,000 drawings and graphics. In imposingly designed rooms, paintings from across seven centuries are presented, from the 14th century to the present day. Many of these are true masterpieces of European art. Would you like to hear some name dropping? Here you go: Hieronymus Bosch, Lucas Cranach, Albrecht Dürer and Sandro Botticelli are represented there, as are Francis Bacon, Gerhard Richter and Wolfgang Tillmans. A real crowd-pleaser is "Goethe in the Roman Campagna" by J. H. Wilhelm Tischbein, probably the best-known painting of the Frankfurt-born Prince of Poets. Those who prefer a more modern approach are likely to enjoy the Goethe silkscreen created by Andy Warhol. Speaking of modern: although these works of art are antique, the museum curators rely on modern apps to serve as audio guides, as well as podcasts, a large digital library with details on each painting, and innovative events including art t

Conversions, renovations, expansions: these things happen regularly in museums, but it is rare for a completely new museum to be commissioned. In 2017, this happened anew with the Barberini Art Museum in Potsdam, which 'The Guardian' immediately ranked among the most important openings of the year internationally. Its prominent location in the new historical centre of Potsdam is particularly noteworthy, as the 18th-century Barberini Palace, which was destroyed in the Second World War, was lavishly reconstructed in the classicist-baroque style. Patron and SAP co-founder Hasso Plattner invested heavily in this, and in a total of 17 exhibition halls, all equipped with the latest technology and featuring high ceilings. Exactly how much is not known. It is also difficult to put a figure on the treasures of the Hasso Plattner Foundation on display across 2,200 square metres. Fact: this permanent exhibition is of great value on its own, being shown alongside high-calibre temporary exhibitions. It focuses on works of French Impressionism and Post-Impressionism; there are around three dozen works by Claude Monet alone (highlight: the Haystacks series). Another focus is on GDR art. These include works by Gerhard Richter as well as by the founders of the Leipzig School, such as Werner Tübke, Bernhard Heisig and Wolfgang Mattheuer. A monumental cast of his sculpture "Step of Century" adorns the museum's inner courtyard.

The Kunstareal in Maxvorstadt is home to a cluster of top-class museums. Internationally best known are the three Pinakothek museums, where visitors can admire great art from the 13th century to the present day. The Alte Pinakothek, which was the largest museum building in the world when it opened in 1836, contains, nominally speaking, the comparatively oldest works. And what a collection it is! For example, Altdorfer's legendary "The Battle of Alexander at Issus", Dürer's famous self-portrait, Leonardo da Vinci's youthful work "Madonna of the Carnation" and "The Great Last Judgement" by Rubens. At over six metres high, it is the largest painting by this brilliant artist. Masterpieces of no lesser importance, but dating from the late 18th to the early 20th century – including works by Klimt, Manet, Goya, Van Gogh – are part of the collection of the Neue Pinakothek (currently under renovation). As if these two renowned museums were not enough, the Pinakothek Modern, opened in 2002, now brings the total to four. Within the bright, classically sleek building is the Modern Art Collection, with numerous paintings from the 20th and 21st centuries (including works by Paul Klee, Franz Marc and Ernst Ludwig Kirchner), the Architecture Museum, the State Collection of Prints and Drawings and the New Collection, which is one of the most important design departments in the world.

Speaking of Dresden, the capital of Saxony is another hotspot for fans of culture owing to the Old Masters Picture Gallery, which is housed in the Zwinger a Baroque palatial complex. This collection of 300 paintings from the 15th to 18th centuries is considered to be one of the most significant of its kind. If you need proof, look no further than The Sistine Madonna by Raphael, one of the most famous paintings of the Italian Renaissance.

The excellent reputations of many other art museums entice culture fans from all over the world to visit Germany. The three Pinakothek museums in Munich, for example, house countless works from the Renaissance to the modern era. The Städel Museum on Frankfurt am Main's Museum Embankment features works dating back as far as the Late Middle Ages. Visitors to this museum can marvel at impactful oil paintings by Albrecht Dürer and Hieronymus Bosch, alongside thousands of photographs and the works of Gerhard Richter, one of the highest-paid living artists. Cologne's Museum Ludwig safeguards the largest collection of American pop art outside of the USA and the world's third-largest Picasso collection.

Frankfurt/Main: Städel Museum

**Alte Pinakothek Munich** More than 700 European paintings from the 14th to 18th centuries are on display at the Alte Pinakothek gallery in Munich – and that's just in the permanent exhibition. The historical museum building is considered to be pioneering for its time. Learn more

**Art Museum in the Monastery of our Lady Magdeburg** The Art Museum in the Monastery of our Lady is located at the heart of Magdeburg, just a stone's throw from the Elbe River. The building complex is considered to be one of the most important examples of Romanesque architecture in the whole of Germany. Learn more

**Brandhorst Museum Munich** The impressive collection on display at the Brandhorst Museum includes more than 1,200 works produced by international artists between the late 1950s and the present day. Learn more

The Sprengel Museum Hannover is delighted to announce a generous donation: the artist Anton Henning has given the museum nine additional works. From 14 October 2026, the new acquisitions will be on view for the first time alongside works already in the collection.

Image: Interieur mit Blumenstilleben und Früchten, No.17, 2024, Öl auf Leinwand, 240 x 260 cm; © VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026; Foto: Herling/Herling/Werner, Sprengel Museum Hannover

Nevin Aladağ has been awarded the Kurt Schwitters Prize 2026 by the Lower Saxony Sparkassen Foundation. The prize, now being conferred for the fifteenth time, carries a monetary award of €30,000 and includes a comprehensive solo exhibition at the Sprengel Museum Hannover. The award ceremony will take place in autumn 2026.

Hannes Malte Mahler is an artist whose work is as colorful and multifaceted as his heraldic animal—the chameleon. The range of his work is enormous, spanning painting, drawing, and photography, as well as object and performance art, all the way to installations featuring—or lacking—“particles” made of Styrodur, doodles, and other trifles. Added to this are digital drawings that Mahler—exploring the tension between art and commerce—transferred onto colorful T-shirts and tote bags in one of his latest major projects under the title “Mahlerwear. It is art”. At the end of 2026, the Sprengel Museum Hannover will dedicate a comprehensive retrospective to Hannes Malte Mahler, honoring the versatility and uniqueness of his artistic work.

The Sprengel Museum Hannover shows a comprehensively reimagined presentation of its collection. Titled "Mein lieber Schwan!", the new display brings together more than 170 artistic positions from the 20th and 21st centuries across approximately 3,000 square metres and 20 newly designed galleries, creating unexpected encounters and fresh dialogues between artworks.

Image: Schad, Christian, Lotte (Die Berlinerin), 1927/28, Öl auf Holz, 66,2 × 54,5 cm, Sprengel Museum Hannover, Kunstbesitz der Landeshauptstadt Hannover; © VG Bild Kunst, Bonn 2026, Foto: Herling/Herling/Werner, Sprengel Museum Hannover

Developed jointly by the Sprengel Museum Hannover and the Fotomuseum Winterthur (28 February–14 June 2026), the exhibition places Sepuya’s artistic, medial, and political concerns at its center—particularly his engagement with Blackness, the body, and spatiality. The artist himself describes his aims as “thinking anew about the structures of photography, portraiture, and queer sociality” and “recognizing the fundamental position of Blackness as material—or Blackness and darkness as a place from which and into which one looks” (Paul Sepuya).

The Kenyan artist Kaloki Nyamai (born 1985 in Kitui) develops powerful visual worlds in his paintings and immersive installations, where traditional visual references intertwine with contemporary perspectives. Through multi-layered compositions and the intentional layering of shapes, symbols, and materials, Nyamai questions historical narratives and rewrites them from a distinctly present-day viewpoint. In the Calder Room of the Sprengel Museum Hannover, he presents three works that exemplify his artistic practice: they address issues of memory, cultural identity, and power, while simultaneously opening a dialogue between individual experience and collective history. The installation will open together with the exhibition "Horst Antes. A Collection." Kaloki Nyamai will be present.

Every year, the Lower Saxony Foundation honors a leading figure in the region’s art scene with a new volume in its “Contemporary Art” book series. The publications pay tribute to artists who, in most cases, can look back on distinguished careers and substantial bodies of work. Each selected artist is invited to shape and design their monograph according to their own vision. The release of every new volume is accompanied by an exhibition at the Sprengel Museum Hannover. In 2026, the established series will feature Gabriela Jolowicz, born in 1978.

The Stiftung Niedersachsen is awarding the renowned SPECTRUM International Prize for Photography to Norwegian artist Frida Orupabo. The prize, endowed with €15,000, includes a solo exhibition at the Sprengel Museum Hannover as well as an accompanying publication. Bringing together 32 works, some of them large-scale, created between 2018 and 2024, the exhibition runs from 5 April to 20 July 2025. The award ceremony will take place on 4 April 2025 at 7 pm, together with the opening of the exhibition.

In 2027, the MdbK will present three major special exhibitions that span a wide range of themes and artistic styles—from _Wolfgang Mattheuer_ to _Arnold Böcklin_ to _Grace Weaver._ The program will be complemented by two very different photography exhibitions: _Photography as Object_ and a presentation of photographs by _Ursula Arnold_. Next year, the MdbK will once again serve as a venue for the _Leipzig Children’s and Youth Art Exhibition_. The established series _Graphic Art in Focus_ will continue. More information is available here.

The permanent exhibition features a portrait of Russian Tsar Peter the Great, on loan from the University of Leipzig’s art collection. It is displayed alongside a painting by Johann Kupetzky (1667–1740) from 1711/12. Comparing the two works offers a fascinating insight into studio practices of the early 18th century. You can learn more about this at the exhibition.

The MdbK preserves the extensive collection of the Leipzig merchant Maximilian Freiherr Speck von Sternburg (1776-1856), which he assembled on his estate in Lützschena near Leipzig. It includes more than 200 paintings, numerous drawings and works of graphic art as well as a library.

The Evelyn Richter and Ursula Arnold Archive is a joint project of the Ostdeutsche Sparkassenstiftung and the Museum der bildenden Künste Leipzig. The works of the photographers are preserved and researched at the MdbK and made public through exhibitions and publications.

# Classical Art Museums: Genuine Masterpieces

The fact that some of the works in art museums are several centuries old does not mean that they are just dusty cultural artefacts. On the contrary! Most museums display their treasures to their best advantage, be it in refurbished spaces or via digital media devices.

Almost every visitor to Dresden has the Zwinger on their itinerary. No wonder, since the impressive building complex is one of Germany's most important baroque buildings. Not to mention the interior features! The Old Masters Art Gallery housed here is one of the most renowned collections of paintings in the world. The "Who's Who" of painting, from Peter Paul Rubens to Albrecht Dürer, is gathered across three floors, focusing in particular on the Renaissance period. More than 300 paintings from across the 15th to 18th centuries, including Vermeer's "The Procuress", Correggio's "Nativity", Titian's "Sleeping Venus" and Raphael's "Sistine Madonna" with its two iconic angels, are on display in the gallery's high, light-filled rooms. The collections of pastels by Rosalba Carriera and paintings by Lucas Cranach are also unique. The goal is to linger instead of rushing through. Especially since the museum has really smartened itself up in 2020. In addition to the careful but decisive modernisation of the building, numerous works were restored, and frames freshly gilded or recreated from scratch. Additionally, extensive accent lighting allows paintings and sculptures to appear literally in the best possible light. A special highlight of the newly-designed Semper Gallery is the integration of the renowned so-called Sculpture Collection, with sculptural works spanning five millennia, from Assyrian relief panels to valuable terracottas and vases.

Frankfurt is not only a financial centre, but also a museum capital. A phenomenal 38 exhibition venues, from the Film Museum to the Architecture Museum to the Jewish Museum, make up the "Museumsufer Frankfurt", an unparalleled cultural hotspot. Right in the middle: the Städel Museum, one of the most important art museums in the country. Founded in 1815 by the banker and merchant Johann Friedrich Städel, the museum collection is the oldest and most renowned in the country. Over the years, it has collected more than 3,100 paintings, 660 sculptures, 5,000 photographs and over 100,000 drawings and graphics. In imposingly designed rooms, paintings from across seven centuries are presented, from the 14th century to the present day. Many of these are true masterpieces of European art. Would you like to hear some name dropping? Here you go: Hieronymus Bosch, Lucas Cranach, Albrecht Dürer and Sandro Botticelli are represented there, as are Francis Bacon, Gerhard Richter and Wolfgang Tillmans. A real crowd-pleaser is "Goethe in the Roman Campagna" by J. H. Wilhelm Tischbein, probably the best-known painting of the Frankfurt-born Prince of Poets. Those who prefer a more modern approach are likely to enjoy the Goethe silkscreen created by Andy Warhol. Speaking of modern: although these works of art are antique, the museum curators rely on modern apps to serve as audio guides, as well as podcasts, a large digital library with details on each painting, and innovative events including art t

Conversions, renovations, expansions: these things happen regularly in museums, but it is rare for a completely new museum to be commissioned. In 2017, this happened anew with the Barberini Art Museum in Potsdam, which 'The Guardian' immediately ranked among the most important openings of the year internationally. Its prominent location in the new historical centre of Potsdam is particularly noteworthy, as the 18th-century Barberini Palace, which was destroyed in the Second World War, was lavishly reconstructed in the classicist-baroque style. Patron and SAP co-founder Hasso Plattner invested heavily in this, and in a total of 17 exhibition halls, all equipped with the latest technology and featuring high ceilings. Exactly how much is not known. It is also difficult to put a figure on the treasures of the Hasso Plattner Foundation on display across 2,200 square metres. Fact: this permanent exhibition is of great value on its own, being shown alongside high-calibre temporary exhibitions. It focuses on works of French Impressionism and Post-Impressionism; there are around three dozen works by Claude Monet alone (highlight: the Haystacks series). Another focus is on GDR art. These include works by Gerhard Richter as well as by the founders of the Leipzig School, such as Werner Tübke, Bernhard Heisig and Wolfgang Mattheuer. A monumental cast of his sculpture "Step of Century" adorns the museum's inner courtyard.

## The Pinakotheks in Munich: Masterpieces Around Every Corner

**Munich: Pinakothek of Modern Art** ©www.nicanorgarcia.com (Nicanor Garcia)

The Kunstareal in Maxvorstadt is home to a cluster of top-class museums. Internationally best known are the three Pinakothek museums, where visitors can admire great art from the 13th century to the present day. The Alte Pinakothek, which was the largest museum building in the world when it opened in 1836, contains, nominally speaking, the comparatively oldest works. And what a collection it is! For example, Altdorfer's legendary "The Battle of Alexander at Issus", Dürer's famous self-portrait, Leonardo da Vinci's youthful work "Madonna of the Carnation" and "The Great Last Judgement" by Rubens. At over six metres high, it is the largest painting by this brilliant artist. Masterpieces of no lesser importance, but dating from the late 18th to the early 20th century – including works by Klimt, Manet, Goya, Van Gogh – are part of the collection of the Neue Pinakothek (currently under renovation). As if these two renowned museums were not enough, the Pinakothek Modern, opened in 2002, now brings the total to four. Within the bright, classically sleek building is the Modern Art Collection, with numerous paintings from the 20th and 21st centuries (including works by Paul Klee, Franz Marc and Ernst Ludwig Kirchner), the Architecture Museum, the State Collection of Prints and Drawings and the New Collection, which is one of the most important design departments in the world.

- **17/07/2026 - 10/10/2027**\\ \\ **Klarenbeek & Dros**\\ \\ Design of the Unusual\\ \\ To the Exhibition\\ \\ Design\\ \\ Design

Housing four museums under one roof devoted to art, works on paper, architecture and design, the Pinakothek der Moderne ranks as one of the greatest collectors of artworks in Europe. Its trans-disciplinary approach – as expressed in its concept of “four-in-one” – is both visionary and, for the most part, unique.

Four museums under one roof present exhibitions of pioneering international architects, designers and artists of the highest quality. Regardless of age, gender, origin or social background, the Pinakothek der Moderne brings people together, encourages reflection, promotes social discourse and conveys education and values. An open meeting place with activities of all kinds in and around the building - sophisticated, inviting, entertaining.

We want to create new encounters, encourage people to join in and make the four museums with art, prints & drawings, architecture and design an experience for everyone. Our programme invites visitors of all ages to discover the collections and special exhibitions of the Pinakothek der Moderne in diverse and creative ways and to gain new perspectives.

The Pinakothek der Moderne app is the digital companion for a new experience, whether before, during or after a visit to the museum - in addition to themed walks through all four collections, the app offers lots of inspiration and information on over 100 objects and over 80 artists, architects and designers.

© Pinakothek der Moderne 2026

Futuro Haus in front of the Pinakothek der Moderne in the Kunstareal in Munich

If it's new approaches to art you're after, Germany is the right place for you. Large exhibition venues present well-known and lesser-known artists with innovative concepts, while permanent exhibitions at art museums provide overviews and insights into a wide variety of stylistic periods. Even gigantic examples of industrial culture become impressive stages for art exhibitions and galleries.

Germany is home to a wealth of spectacular museums and exhibition venues. Built by Mies van der Rohe, the New National Gallery in Berlin, with its glass main building and underground exhibition rooms, is a work of art in itself. In Munich, the Pinakothek museums are impressive, with their broad spectrum of antique sculptures, photography and modern paintings. Culture and entertainment are combined in Berlin's new Deutschlandmuseum in Berlin, which brings German history to life in an immersive way.

Germany's art academies, which support talented young people, are also an important foundation for the vibrancy of the German art scene. The Berlin University of the Artsis one of the largest art academies in Europe, with a range of courses in fine arts, music, performing arts and design. One of the oldest and most prestigious art academies in Germany is the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. World-famous artists such as Wassily Kandinsky, Ernst Barlach and Giorgio de Chirico studied here.

Conservation in Action: Documenting Crawford Art Gallery’s Collection (Recording)

Crawford Art Gallery is one of Ireland’s National Cultural Institutions, charged with the care of over 3,500 diverse artworks from the National Collection, from 18th century Irish and European painting and sculpture, through to contemporary video installations.

In 2024, Crawford Art Gallery embarked on an ambitious redevelopment project, Transforming Crawford Art Gallery, to ensure the gallery’s historic buildings in the heart of Cork city are conserved and enhanced for generations to come.

From 22 September 2024, Crawford Art Gallery is temporarily closed to the public to facilitate these redevelopment works. Gallery staff continue to work behind the scenes, caring for the collection, organising an offsite programme of Learn & Explore events, and preparing for reopening in 2028.

Crawford Art Gallery is delighted to loan three objects from its decorative art collection to Emo Court.

Displayed within the fine interior of Emo Court, the three objects on loan are: an **Empire style chair**, once owned by art collector Hugh Lane at his Cheyne Walk home in London, with lion-head armrest terminals. It was presented to Crawford Art Gallery by the Friends of the National Collections of Ireland (FNCI) in 1960; a large **alabaster urn** with Bacchanalian motifs that once stood on the windowsill of Crawford Art Gallery’s main staircase and, subsequently, in its wood-panelled library; and a mahogany **Georgian sofa table**, formerly owned by the Penrose family of Woodhill, Cork, which has shallow drawers, foldable leaves, and castors. It has been in the collection since 2008 when it was presented as part of the Cooper Penrose Collection by John and Helena Mooney.

Crawford Art Gallery wishes to thank the OPW team at Emo Court.

Fourteen works of Irish art from the collection of Crawford Art Gallery are on loan to Hillsborough Castle (Historic Royal Palaces) for a period of three years.

Dating to the eighteenth-century and open to the public, Hillsborough Castle is an official British royal residence set within 100 acres of picturesque gardens in County Down, Northern Ireland. It is here that the Hillsborough Agreement was signed on 5 February 2010.

The fourteen works on loan from Crawford Art Gallery are displayed in the historic State Drawing Room. Each painting is by a twentieth-century artist with a strong connection to the north of Ireland, including Margaret Clarke, Gerard Dillon, Paul Henry, and Jack B. Yeats.

Coincidentally, the family of our namesake, William Horatio Crawford (1812-1888), was originally from nearby Crawfordsburn, County Down. Settling in Cork in the late eighteenth-century, they co-established the Beamish & Crawford brewery and became significant philanthropists and supporters of education and the arts.

Crawford Art Gallery wishes to thank David Orr, Emma Lawthers, and the teams at Hillsborough Castle and Historic Royal Palaces.

Highlanes Gallery is a public art gallery and visual arts exhibition centre in Drogheda, Ireland.The gallery opened its doors on October 4, 2006 and was the culmination of many years planning to deliver a dedicated visual arts space for the Irish north east region, of an International standard in terms of design, management and environmental control.

Originally developed by artist Bea Orpen, Husband Terry Trench, and the 1947 Museum Committee, the Drogheda Municipal Art Collection has grown to include more than 100 artworks. The centrepiece of Kilkenny’s medieval footprint is Kilkenny Castle, built by the Normans and standing tall over the Marble City for over 800 years. Join a tour to learn about the powerful and wealthy Butler family, who ruled as the earls, marquesses and dukes of Ormond for six centuries – and turned Kilkenny into a regional powerhouse. On your tour, check out intriguing interiors like the delicate Chinese wallpaper in the ladies’ withdrawing room and the hand-painted roof in the Picture Gallery, decorated with Pre-Raphaelite ladies and naturalistic scenes.

Experience a selection of Irish design and crafts at the Kilkenny Design Centre, across the street from the castle. Take in this showcase of Irish and contemporary gifts, and shop for a memento from your trip or a gift for a loved one. You’ll find pottery produced by Nicholas Mosse, Enibas jewellery designed by Sabina Lenz, work by artist Sharon McDaid and more.

Next door, the Castle Yard hosts a number of talented craft and design businesses from Kilkenny and beyond. Discover the breadth of work that goes into each design and watch craftspeople at work, then pop over to the National Design & Craft Gallery, featuring exhibitions across a wide variety of media, including textile, glass and ceramics.

Once you've satisfied your thirst, explore the collection of 20th-century Irish art for free at the Butler Gallery. Alongside their permanent collections, discover their contemporary exhibitions, which reflect evolving visual art practices and the use of different media. Outside, feel free to wander the romantic secret garden and see contemporary Irish sculpture.

# Limerick City Gallery of Art

Limerick City, Co. Limerick

Limerick City Gallery of Art in Limerick City, invites you to see the best of contemporary art through the temporary exhibition programme and to enjoy the permanent collection of 19th and 20th century Irish art.

Limerick City Gallery of Art LCGA in Limerick City, is one of the leading contemporary art galleries in Ireland and is home to an important collection of Irish 18th to 21st century art in all media. It has the National Collection of Contemporary Drawing and the Michael O’Connor International Poster Collection part of its collections. The Permanent Collection is exhibited on a rotation basis throughout the year in its dedicated exhibition gallery.

Artists within the Permanent Collection are Paul Henry, Jack B. Yeats, Sean Keating, Charles Lamb, Letita Hamilton, Grace Henry, Sarah Purser, Walter Verling, Donald Teskey, John Shinnors, and many more. LCGA hosts around 8 contemporary exhibits per year with Irish and International artists and hosts EVA International, Ireland's biennial of contemporary art.

LCGA is housed in the Carnegie Building, on the grounds of the People’s Park in the centre of Limerick City. Limerick City Gallery of Art is fully accessible with a ramp at the front entrance, wide doorways, a lift and disabled toilet facilities.

## The Family of Man au Château de Clervaux

**La collection *The Family of Man* se compose de 503 photographies de 273 auteurs originaires de 68 pays, rassemblées par Edward Steichen pour le Museum of Modern Art de New York (MoMA).**

Présentée pour la première fois en 1955, l'exposition se veut un manifeste pour la paix et l'égalité fondamentale des hommes à travers la photographie humaniste d'après-guerre. Les images d'auteurs tels que Robert Capa, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Dorothea Lange, Robert Doisneau, August Sander, Ansel Adams, ... sont mises en scène d'une manière moderniste et spectaculaire.

Après un voyage autour du monde dans plus de 160 musées, la dernière version intégrale de l'exposition est installée en 1994 au Château de Clervaux de façon permanente.

Edward Steichen visite son pays natal et exprime le vœu que "The Family of Man" soit exposée de façon permanente au Château de Clervaux. Le gouvernement américain fait don de la dernière version intégrale itinérante au Luxembourg.

exposition partielle des photographies au Château de Clervaux

Installation de la collection en tant qu'exposition permanente au Château de Clervaux

Exposer aujourd'hui ce patrimoine demande de respecter l'histoire et d'observer une position quasi archéologique : le parcours de l'exposition et la chronologie des images ont été respectées et s'alignent sur la mise en scène de l'originale présentée au MoMA afin de pouvoir restituer l'expérience du visiteur et l'impact que les images exercent sur lui. Cette approche requiert cependant une distance prise par rapport à l'histoire qui se traduit à Clervaux par une architecture très sobre des salles d'exposition qui a été conçue par la muséographe Nathalie Jacoby du bureau NJOY. Par ailleurs, une nouvelle approche de médiation fait partie du concept d'exposition qui comprend p.ex. une nouvelle bibliothèque muséale et un parcours via tablette numérique (Ipad mini). Le visiteur sera ainsi accompagné dans sa visite et aura accès à une documentation sur l'histoire de l'exposition initiale, son parcours, les photographes de *The Family of Man* et sur Edward Steichen.

*©Pancake! Photographie*

**Immerse yourself in the fascinating world of "The Family of Man" photo exhibition in Clervaux! Be inspired by this unique collection that captures the life, cultures and emotions of mankind in breathtaking images!**

With over 10 million visitors since its creation, the world-famous photo exhibition "The Family of Man" is a legend in the history of photography. Created by Edward Steichen and presented for the first time in 1955 at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, it is considered a manifesto for peace and human equality, expressed through post-war humanist photography. The collection consists of a total of 503 photographs by 273 photographers from 68 countries. After travelling through more than 150 museums worldwide, the last complete version of "The Family of Man" is housed as a permanent exhibition at Clervaux Castle since 1994. Since 2003 it figures on the UNESCO World Documentary Heritage list.

Beautiful Museum van Loon, a private residence built in 1672, offers a glimpse into the lives of the wealthy in the Golden Age. And the Our Lord in the Attic museum in Amsterdam is a fascinating monument hidden in the attic of a 17th-century canal house: a clandestine church from the time of the Protestant Reformation, when catholic church services were banned.

Dutch history is inextricably intertwined with seafaring and trade, and Amsterdam’s National Maritime Museum presents 500 years of Dutch maritime history. Furthermore, a dive into the Netherlands’ past is not complete without learning about the country’s experience of the Second World War, German occupation, persecution of Jews and other groups, and the resistance. Make sure to add the following to your travel agenda: the Freedom Museum (Groesbeek), the Dutch Resistance Museum (Amsterdam), the Overloon War Museum (Overloon) and the Airborne Museum Hartenstein (Oosterbeek).

Of course, you can visit famous venues such as the Rijksmuseum, the Stedelijk Museum and the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, the Mauritshuis in The Hague or Rotterdam’s Boijmans van Beunigen. However, don’t overlook other locations. The Netherlands is home to over 120 art collections. In Wassenaar, stroll through the sculpture gardens of Museum Voorlinden and take in their stunning selection of contemporary art.

Enjoy the wonderful surroundings of the Kröller-Müller, which includes a significant Van Gogh collection and a remarkable sculpture garden. In Haarlem, just a stone’s throw from Amsterdam, you can say hello to Haarlem’s own Old Master at the Frans Hals Museum. And for a closer look at the life of Vincent Van Gogh, visit the artist’s hometown of Nuenen in North Brabant at the Van Gogh Village Museum.

From biology and physics to engineering and space exploration, don your thinking cap at a science museum – big names include Amsterdam’s NEMO and Leiden’s Naturalis. Did you know that the Netherlands is a world leader in scientific research? To maintain this, the Dutch government invests heavily in this sector (over €4.5 billion per year) to maintain this reputation. Discover the long-standing dedication to this field during your trip.

Is the city of Leiden on your list? If so, stop by Rijksmuseum Boerhaave to learn more about the history of medicine and scientific accomplishments. Or take a trip to the stars at Space Expo Noordwijk, where you will uncover the secrets of space travel and out-of-this-world scientific innovations. And for an interactive experience for the whole family, stop by GeoFort in Herwijnen. On this fortress island, learn more about our planet through hands-on activities while also delving into some local natural history.

Alongside the art or science museums that you might expect to see, there are also numerous offbeat locations that are worth exploring. If you are interested in experiencing something a little bit different, these hidden gems could make for a memorable day out. Take The Cat Cabinet, for example, located in a stunning canal house in the city center of Amsterdam. It is here you will find a treasure trove of cat-themed paintings, sculptures and more in this personal family collection that also features works by Pablo Picasso and Rembrandt.

If you are more of a foodie, head to the city of Alkmaar to the Cheese Museum. You might have already guessed it, but here you can learn about the history of Dutch cheese, see how it’s made and even taste some samples – yummy! Or swing by Museum Speelklok in Utrecht. A great activity for kids, this museum features a huge range of self-playing instruments, from music boxes to street organs. And if that has tickled your fancy, Amsterdam’s Pianola Museum, which is wholly dedicated to the self-playing player piano, might be for you.

October 10, 2026 until January 17, 2027

*Some Wild Kind of Language* is Adam Pendleton’s first museum exhibition in the Netherlands, and features ten paintings and eight large-scale drawings. The exhibition showcases Pendleton’s exploration of abstract forms. Many of the works are new and have never been shown before, making the exhibition a milestone in his body of work.

Installed within the central spaces of the museum's historic building, *Some Wild Kind of Language* positions the Stedelijk's architecture and collection as active components of the exhibition. In the iconic staircase of the museum's 1895 building, Pendleton engages one of its most historically significant spaces. In 1938, curator Willem Sandberg painted the staircase's dark-colored brick walls white to establish one of the earliest "white cubes," a transformation he later extended throughout the museum after becoming director in 1945. Pendleton transforms the staircase into a "black cube" for the presentation of a new body of work: eight monumental Basis drawings. These are the largest drawings Pendleton has completed to date.

Pendleton's painting process begins on paper, where he explores the full breadth of mark-making. He layers paint, spray paint, ink, and watercolor, integrating graffiti-like marks, fragmentary text, and geometric forms, often through stenciling techniques. These works on paper are documented and subsequently layered through a screen-printing process that deliberately moves between—and generatively conflates—the manual and the mechanical, rethinking how paintings can be made through successive stages of translation and transformation. Across the exhibition, paintings and drawings unfold through a distilled layering of gesture, fragment, and form. Rather than centering on a single visual moment, Pendleton creates continuous, expansive fields—an "all-over" condition—that challenge conventional expectations of composition.

Pendleton's paintings, installed in the IMC Gallery, also known as the Gallery of Honour, occupy an important position within the museum's historical and contemporary collections. Bringing together works of different scales—including a painting measuring nearly six meters wide—the exhibition creates an encounter between Pendleton's practice and the histories of Minimalism, Conceptual art, and post-war abstraction represented in the museum's collection. Pendleton's *Black Dada, Days,* and monumental *WE ARE NOT* paintings can be understood both as a continuation of and a response to the large-scale works by artists such as Barnett Newman, Morris Louis, and other North American Color Field and Minimal painters that the Stedelijk historically presented in the same gallery.

Adam Pendleton (1984, Richmond, Virginia, United States), a central figure in contemporary American art, is known for paintings that push the boundaries of the medium through a sustained engagement with process, language, and conceptual form. In 2008, he began to define the working method for which he is now widely recognized as Black Dada—a critical framework that explores the relationship between Blackness, abstraction, and avant-garde movements.

In 2024, he was honored with the Rosenthal Family Foundation Award for Painting from the American Academy of Arts and Letters. Pendleton’s work is held in numerous public collections, including The Museum of Modern Art, New York; the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York; the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Washington, DC; the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago; Tate, London; and the Pinakothek der Moderne, Munich.

Beautiful Museum van Loon, a private residence built in 1672, offers a glimpse into the lives of the wealthy in the Golden Age. And the Our Lord in the Attic museum in Amsterdam is a fascinating monument hidden in the attic of a 17th-century canal house: a clandestine church from the time of the Protestant Reformation, when catholic church services were banned.

Dutch history is inextricably intertwined with seafaring and trade, and Amsterdam’s National Maritime Museum presents 500 years of Dutch maritime history. Furthermore, a dive into the Netherlands’ past is not complete without learning about the country’s experience of the Second World War, German occupation, persecution of Jews and other groups, and the resistance. Make sure to add the following to your travel agenda: the Freedom Museum (Groesbeek), the Dutch Resistance Museum (Amsterdam), the Overloon War Museum (Overloon) and the Airborne Museum Hartenstein (Oosterbeek).

Of course, you can visit famous venues such as the Rijksmuseum, the Stedelijk Museum and the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, the Mauritshuis in The Hague or Rotterdam’s Boijmans van Beunigen. However, don’t overlook other locations. The Netherlands is home to over 120 art collections. In Wassenaar, stroll through the sculpture gardens of Museum Voorlinden and take in their stunning selection of contemporary art.

Enjoy the wonderful surroundings of the Kröller-Müller, which includes a significant Van Gogh collection and a remarkable sculpture garden. In Haarlem, just a stone’s throw from Amsterdam, you can say hello to Haarlem’s own Old Master at the Frans Hals Museum. And for a closer look at the life of Vincent Van Gogh, visit the artist’s hometown of Nuenen in North Brabant at the Van Gogh Village Museum.

From biology and physics to engineering and space exploration, don your thinking cap at a science museum – big names include Amsterdam’s NEMO and Leiden’s Naturalis. Did you know that the Netherlands is a world leader in scientific research? To maintain this, the Dutch government invests heavily in this sector (over €4.5 billion per year) to maintain this reputation. Discover the long-standing dedication to this field during your trip.

Alongside the art or science museums that you might expect to see, there are also numerous offbeat locations that are worth exploring. If you are interested in experiencing something a little bit different, these hidden gems could make for a memorable day out. Take The Cat Cabinet, for example, located in a stunning canal house in the city center of Amsterdam. It is here you will find a treasure trove of cat-themed paintings, sculptures and more in this personal family collection that also features works by Pablo Picasso and Rembrandt.

If you are more of a foodie, head to the city of Alkmaar to the Cheese Museum. You might have already guessed it, but here you can learn about the history of Dutch cheese, see how it’s made and even taste some samples – yummy! Or swing by Museum Speelklok in Utrecht. A great activity for kids, this museum features a huge range of self-playing instruments, from music boxes to street organs. And if that has tickled your fancy, Amsterdam’s Pianola Museum, which is wholly dedicated to the self-playing player piano, might be for you.

# Visit the Dordrechts Museum in Dordrecht

Located in the historic city of Dordrecht, Dordrechts Museum is one of the oldest art museums in the Netherlands. Discover six centuries of Dutch painting, renowned artists, temporary exhibitions and one of the country's most important art collections.

Vaste collectie Dordrechts Museum

**Dordrechts Museum** - 6 centuries of Dutch art with a permanent collection and temporary exhibitions.  
**Huis Van Gijn** - step back into the 19th century and see how upstairs and downstairs lived and worked.  
**Hof van Nederland** - a historical museum in which you experience how we, in the Netherlands, deal with our freedoms, then and now, told from different perspectives. For children there is a ball pool, an escape game and a special Griffioen tour.

## What is the Dordrechts Museum famous for?

The Dordrechts Museum is one of the oldest art museums in the Netherlands. It is known for its extensive collection of Dutch paintings spanning six centuries, from Old Masters to modern and contemporary art. The museum is particularly renowned for works connected to Dordrecht and the Dutch Golden Age.

Dordrecht is easily accessible from Amsterdam and Rotterdam by train. From Dordrecht railway station, the historic city centre and the Dordrechts Museum can be reached by public transport, bicycle or on foot. Dordrecht is also accessible by car and waterbus, a perfect option if you come from Rotterdam.

In addition to the Dordrechts Museum, visitors can explore the historic city centre of Dordrecht, the Huis Van Gijn museum and the Hof van Nederland. The city is known for its historic architecture, canals, cultural attractions, shops, restaurants and waterfront views.

A perfect day in Dordrecht starts with a visit to the Dordrechts Museum, followed by a walk through the historic city centre. You can also visit Huis Van Gijn or Hof van Nederland, enjoy lunch at a local café, browse independent shops and discover the city from the water.

Groninger Museum holds over 60,000 artworks and objects spanning five millennia, mirroring a similar polyphonic nerve to its architecture. Just as the building was a postmodern provocation built on collaboration by multiple architects and designers, the collection holds the same instinct.

Studio Alchimia, Jasje, 1989, Collection Groninger Museum

Masanori Umeda, Tawaraya ring, 1981, Collection Groninger Museum

Fluxus, Fluxus presents: Fluxus Symphony Orchestra in Fluxus Concert, Carnegie Recital Hall, 1964, Collection Groninger Museum

Studio Alchimia and Memphis treated design as a form of cultural critique. An early acquisition of Fluxus set the museum on a path to dissolve the line between art and everyday life. Groninger Museum also holds the largest collection of De Ploeg, a movement that built a radical identity against conservatism and toward open, international dialogue. Each of these movements asked timely questions related to what happens when boundaries between disciplines are dissolved.

Our exhibition making and publications connect to the polyphonic nature of the collection, from Vincent van Gogh to Nathalie Du Pasquier, from Song dynasty vases to Rineke Dijkstra, Marga Weimans or Odilon Redon. Our programme is in resonance with impulses found in the fashion of Viktor & Rolf and Iris van Herpen, the bold design of Swip Stolk, Hendrik Nicolaas Werkman’s typographical experiments, and architecture by Zaha Hadid - to name a few.

Exceptional museums throughout the Netherlands showcase the versatility of Dutch art. The Groninger Museum is home to groundbreaking design, while Museum Arnhem highlights contemporary themes. The Singer Laren museum and concert hall in Laren links modernism with nature and culture, and Beelden aan Zee in Scheveningen is all about sculptures on the coast. In short, wherever you are in our beautiful country, you will always find museums to pique your interest.

Dutch art and artists are known the world over. Home to Rembrandt, Vermeer, Van Gogh, Mondrian and many others, the Netherlands is often recognized as a ‘land of painters’. From the Old Masters of the Dutch Era (also known as the Dutch Golden Age) to modern icons and contemporary art installations, there is so much to see during your time here.

Of course, you can visit famous venues such as the Rijksmuseum, the Stedelijk Museum and the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, the Mauritshuis in The Hague or Rotterdam’s Boijmans van Beunigen. However, don’t overlook other locations. The Netherlands is home to over 120 art collections. In Wassenaar, stroll through the sculpture gardens of Museum Voorlinden and take in their stunning selection of contemporary art.

Enjoy the wonderful surroundings of the Kröller-Müller, which includes a significant Van Gogh collection and a remarkable sculpture garden. In Haarlem, just a stone’s throw from Amsterdam, you can say hello to Haarlem’s own Old Master at the Frans Hals Museum. And for a closer look at the life of Vincent Van Gogh, visit the artist’s hometown of Nuenen in North Brabant at the Van Gogh Village Museum.

Alongside the art or science museums that you might expect to see, there are also numerous offbeat locations that are worth exploring. If you are interested in experiencing something a little bit different, these hidden gems could make for a memorable day out. Take The Cat Cabinet, for example, located in a stunning canal house in the city center of Amsterdam. It is here you will find a treasure trove of cat-themed paintings, sculptures and more in this personal family collection that also features works by Pablo Picasso and Rembrandt.

## at the Princessehof Ceramics Museum

Welcome to the Princessehof Ceramics Museum, an 18th-century city palace in the middle of Leeuwarden's historic city centre.

### Opening hours

Special opening hours: Easter Monday, Whit Monday and Boxing Day  
Closed: On New Year's Day, King's Day (27 April) and Christmas Day

Discover the rich collection, focusing on Asian, European and modern ceramics. The musuem holds the largest and most varied collection of Chinese porcelain in the Netherlands and shows a rich a multifaceted picture of Dutch art nouveau and art deco ceramics from the period 1880-1930.

The Princessehof strives to be as accessible as possible to all visitors. Housed in an old building, the museum is easily accessible for the disabled. Parking is easy in the car park next to the museum. Click here for more information on accessibility at the museum. We wish you a pleasant visit. To protect our collection, we ask you to pay attention to some house rules. Click here for more information on our house rules.

The Princessehof is located in the middle of Leeuwarden's beautiful historic city centre, a ten-minute walk from the train and bus station. You enter the museum through the museum shop, there is also an entrance on the Groeneweg where you walk into the museum through the renovated palace garden. Click here for more information on the route.

# The Kröller-Müller Museum

The Kröller-Müller museum in Gelderland boasts not only a world-famous collection of 19th and 20th century art, but also an immense collection of pieces by Vincent van Gogh. If you’re an art lover and you’re in Gelderland, you cannot afford to miss this chance.

- Discover the Kröller-Müller museum’s splendid sculpture park.
- Take a walk through the 25-acre sculpture park.
- Discover the unique Van Gogh collection.

Helene Kröller-Müller had a dream to create her own ‘museum-home’. With her wealthy husband’s money and help from an advisor, she purchased over 11,500 art objects. The Kröller-Müller Museum opened its doors in 1938 in the Hoge Veluwe National Park.

There’s plenty to see at the Kröller-Müller Museum, but these are the two particularly interesting highlights:

Combine nature and culture by visiting the Kröller-Müller Museum in Hoge Veluwe National Park. If you take one of the free-to-use white bikes, you can enjoy the surroundings in the morning and visit the Kröller-Müller Museum in the afternoon.

- What is the Kröller-Müller Museum?

The Kröller-Müller Museum is a modern art museum. It boast the next-to-largest collection of paintings and drawings by Van Gogh. The collection of 19th and 20th century art embraces top works by celebrated artists, including Claude Monet, Pablo Picasso, and Piet Mondrian. The Kröller-Müller Museum also includes an impressive sculpture garden in the large surrounding park.

The Kröller-Müller Museum is well worth a visit. The museum boasts the world’s biggest private collection of Van Gogh paintings. It also features an impressive permanent collection of 19th and 20th century art. The museum is surrounded by a beautifully maintained park with one of Europe’s biggest sculpture gardens. In short, it is a real must-see museum for art lovers.

Exceptional museums throughout the Netherlands showcase the versatility of Dutch art. The Groninger Museum is home to groundbreaking design, while Museum Arnhem highlights contemporary themes. The Singer Laren museum and concert hall in Laren links modernism with nature and culture, and Beelden aan Zee in Scheveningen is all about sculptures on the coast. In short, wherever you are in our beautiful country, you will always find museums to pique your interest.

Dutch art and artists are known the world over. Home to Rembrandt, Vermeer, Van Gogh, Mondrian and many others, the Netherlands is often recognized as a ‘land of painters’. From the Old Masters of the Dutch Era (also known as the Dutch Golden Age) to modern icons and contemporary art installations, there is so much to see during your time here.

Of course, you can visit famous venues such as the Rijksmuseum, the Stedelijk Museum and the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, the Mauritshuis in The Hague or Rotterdam’s Boijmans van Beunigen. However, don’t overlook other locations. The Netherlands is home to over 120 art collections. In Wassenaar, stroll through the sculpture gardens of Museum Voorlinden and take in their stunning selection of contemporary art.

Enjoy the wonderful surroundings of the Kröller-Müller, which includes a significant Van Gogh collection and a remarkable sculpture garden. In Haarlem, just a stone’s throw from Amsterdam, you can say hello to Haarlem’s own Old Master at the Frans Hals Museum. And for a closer look at the life of Vincent Van Gogh, visit the artist’s hometown of Nuenen in North Brabant at the Van Gogh Village Museum.

Alongside the art or science museums that you might expect to see, there are also numerous offbeat locations that are worth exploring. If you are interested in experiencing something a little bit different, these hidden gems could make for a memorable day out. Take The Cat Cabinet, for example, located in a stunning canal house in the city center of Amsterdam. It is here you will find a treasure trove of cat-themed paintings, sculptures and more in this personal family collection that also features works by Pablo Picasso and Rembrandt.

Discover the Rijksmuseum’s iconic art treasures, the combination of archaeology and art at the Drents Museum, or the ever-changing exhibitions at Kunsthal Rotterdam. And what about the Kröller-Müller Museum in the Veluwe, where nature and art come together, or Singer Laren, where everyone can find a work of art that speaks to them.

The Art Alliance museums invite you to discover the Netherlands through art, stories and encounters. From world-famous masterpieces to surprising contemporary art. From design and photography to history, heritage and remarkable collections in unexpected places. Wherever you find yourself, there’s always another discovery just around the corner.

In The Hague, the Mauritshuis awaits with world-famous masterpieces that attract visitors from across the globe, while Haarlem’s Frans Hals Museum shows just how innovative portraiture can be. Remarkable encounters can also be found off the beaten track. In the historic centre of Dordrecht, the Dordrechts Museum offers a wonderful journey through six centuries of Dutch painting. In the Veluwe National Park, visitors can combine a cycle ride through woods and heathland with a visit to one of the world’s largest Van Gogh collections at the Kröller-Müller Museum.

And that is perhaps the greatest strength of the Dutch Masters: they teach you to look more closely. Not just at the light, colour and details in their paintings, but also at the Netherlands beyond the museum. At the clouds above the landscape, the quiet streets and everyday moments that can suddenly turn into something special.

The Depot of Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen is the world’s first publicly accessible art storage facility.

The Depot of Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen is the world’s first publicly accessible art storage facility. The depot is located next to Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Museumpark in Rotterdam. Visitors can see the result of over 175 years of collecting. More than 155,000 objects housed together, arranged in fourteen storage compartments with five different climates. Next to the objects, all the activities that go into preserving and managing a collection are on open view in the building.

The Depot is known to have dazzling exterior and a spectacular interior. Its roof engulfs you in a green oasis, right in the heart of Rotterdam. It offers spectacular panoramic views of the city and is home to restaurant Renilde, led by chef Jim de Jong. There, an exceptional culinary journey awaits you.

Located in lush green surroundings, it is home to the second-largest collection of the Dutch icon’s work in the world. Want another top tip? Go on a small Van Gogh tour in rural Brabant.

The Kunstmuseum Den Haag, housed in an Art Deco building designed by famous Dutch architect Berlage, houses the largest collection of Piet Mondrian’s work in the world, including the masterpiece *Victory Boogie Woogie*. This museum in The Hague also displays works by Claude Monet, Vincent van Gogh, Pablo Picasso and many other artists.

Characteristically, this representation also attempted to mirror the artist's state of mind. Jozef Israëls was one of the leaders of this movement and many of his works can be found in the Kunstmuseum in The Hague and the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. In Groningen, Israëls’ hometown, there is a monument in memory of him created by sculptor Abraham Hesselink.

The Mauritshuis and the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid join forces for a special exhibition. In this unique exchange, the first-ever between the two museums, the Mauritshuis welcomes twenty-five masterpieces from the world-famous Spanish collection and, in turn, twenty-five gems from The Hague will go on show in Madrid.

The Mauritshuis and the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza are in love and want to shout it from the rooftops! Both museums are simultaneously exchanging 25 masterpieces with one another. The exhibition celebrates the enduring relationship between the two museums, hence the theme of love. Intangible though love is, it’s a universal feeling. And, like us, the people in the paintings experience the spectrum of emotion: from falling in love to the joy of connection, recognition and intimacy. But love is also full of contradictions: the pain of longing, and the sorrow of loss or forbidden intimacy. The paintings may date from the 15th and 16th centuries, but these emotions are timeless.

*Willem van Haecht, Apelles Painting Campaspe, c. 1630 (detail) Mauritshuis*

To coincide with the exhibitions at the Mauritshuis and the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, the publication Thyssen-Bornemisza & Mauritshuis: A love story between two museums is being released.

For this book, the museums invited ten Spanish and ten Dutch authors to write about the paintings from both collections. Inspired by the beauty of the artworks, and drawing on their own perspectives and backgrounds, their starting point was love in all its forms: from love between people and love of nature, to love of art itself. The publication is made possible in part by the Mercura Fund.

Exceptional museums throughout the Netherlands showcase the versatility of Dutch art. The Groninger Museum is home to groundbreaking design, while Museum Arnhem highlights contemporary themes. The Singer Laren museum and concert hall in Laren links modernism with nature and culture, and Beelden aan Zee in Scheveningen is all about sculptures on the coast. In short, wherever you are in our beautiful country, you will always find museums to pique your interest.

Dutch art and artists are known the world over. Home to Rembrandt, Vermeer, Van Gogh, Mondrian and many others, the Netherlands is often recognized as a ‘land of painters’. From the Old Masters of the Dutch Era (also known as the Dutch Golden Age) to modern icons and contemporary art installations, there is so much to see during your time here.

Of course, you can visit famous venues such as the Rijksmuseum, the Stedelijk Museum and the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, the Mauritshuis in The Hague or Rotterdam’s Boijmans van Beunigen. However, don’t overlook other locations. The Netherlands is home to over 120 art collections. In Wassenaar, stroll through the sculpture gardens of Museum Voorlinden and take in their stunning selection of contemporary art.

Enjoy the wonderful surroundings of the Kröller-Müller, which includes a significant Van Gogh collection and a remarkable sculpture garden. In Haarlem, just a stone’s throw from Amsterdam, you can say hello to Haarlem’s own Old Master at the Frans Hals Museum. And for a closer look at the life of Vincent Van Gogh, visit the artist’s hometown of Nuenen in North Brabant at the Van Gogh Village Museum.

Museum Catharijneconvent occupies a characteristic building in the old city centre of Utrecht. The building has a long history going back to the fourteenth century. Originally, it was the site of a shelter for the homeless. In the fifteenth century the Carmelites acquired the land and built a convent. Later, the knights of St John turned it into a hospital, which it remained until the beginning of the nineteenth century. Subsequently it served various other functions until becoming a museum in 1979.

Body. Ideal, Gaze, Freedom – Göteborgs konstmuseum

7 March 2026–17 January 2027

**From the ideals of antiquity to visions of emancipation and freedom. This spring, the Gothenburg Museum of Art presents a major exhibition dedicated to one of art history’s most enduring and fascinating motifs: the human body. *Body. Ideal, Gaze, Freedom* brings together around one hundred works that explore and challenge historical ideals, examine the role of the model, and reveal the body’s expressive and creative potential.**

The exhibition is a meeting ground for periods, styles, and artistic expressions – from paintings, drawings, sculptures, and prints to photography and video art. It offers a sweeping overview of how bodies have been depicted, interpreted, and controlled throughout art history. Most of the works come from the museum’s own collection, featuring artists such as Hanna Pauli, Francis Bacon, and Charlotte Gyllenhammar.

To broaden the presentation, the exhibition also includes significant loans from institutions and private collectors, featuring prominent works by American sculptor Nick Cave and performance artists Ana Mendieta and Hannah Wilke. Contemporary artists such as Ruby Okoro, Sally von Rosen, and Ussi’n Yala contribute new works created in response to the exhibition’s theme.

This autumn, Artipelag presents *INNER CHILD: Playing with Design* – a unique exhibition exploring the inner child as a source of creativity, hope, and the joy of making. An international design exhibition about imagination, playfulness, and preserving the child within us.

The Art Gallery will be open until 6 pm on Thursday–Saturday from December 3–19.

Created exclusively for Artipelag by internationally renowned trend forecaster Lidewij Edelkoort and curator Philip Fimmano, the exhibition brings together the work of one hundred designers and artists in an inspiring narrative about playfulness, imagination, and the human need to create with our hands in an age shaped by rapid technological development and global uncertainty.

On view at Artipelag, 10 October 2026 – 11 April 2027.

In conjunction with *INNER CHILD – Playing with Design*, Artipelag invites you to a program filled with creativity, play, and the joy of making. During the exhibition period, enjoy Afternoon Tea, creative workshops for children and families, and other program events. Come discover, create, and be inspired!

Hallands Konstmuseum (Halland Art Museum) is beautifully situated beside the River Nissan and Norre Katts Park in central Halmstad. Several exhibitions are always on display simultaneously, often drawing on our extensive collection of Halland art. Guided tours are offered every weekend and are included in the admission fee. Explore art as a family! At Hallands Konstmuseum (Halland Art Museum), there are exciting activities for all ages. Listen to our family stories, solve tricky art riddles, or get creative in the studio. There’s always something to discover – no matter your age!

Hallands Konstmuseum (Halland Art Museum) has an extensive and continually growing collection of Halland art, including works by the Halmstadgruppen (Halmstad Group), Thea Ekström, Olle Bærtling and Lotta Antonsson. Discover Sweden’s modern and contemporary art museums, where everything from photography and design to painting and sculpture takes centre stage. From Kiruna in the north to Malmö in the south, you'll find inspiring collections, bold exhibitions and distinctive museum settings.

Since opening in Stockholm in 2010, Fotografiska has expanded to cities including Berlin, Tallinn, Shanghai and Shenzhen. Located on Södermalm, this photography museum has no permanent collection, instead presenting changing exhibitions by established and emerging photographers from around the world. Open until late in the evening, it also hosts talks and events. Round off your visit at the award-winning restaurant, serving seasonal food with panoramic views across the water.

Housed in a former boiler house beneath the Älvsborg Bridge in Gothenburg, Röda Sten Konsthall has a colourful past. Once a venue for rave parties and threatened with demolition, the industrial building is now a hub for contemporary art, showcasing sculpture, installations, photography and video art. The gallery also hosts talks and workshops and organises the Gothenburg International Biennial for Contemporary Art (GIBCA), held across the city. The next edition runs from 4 September to 21 November 2027.

With a focus on contemporary and public art, Borås Konstmuseum showcases Swedish and international artists through painting, sculpture, photography and moving images. Admission is free, and visitors can explore exhibitions, guided tours and creative activities. Since 2008, the museum has organised the Borås International Sculpture Biennial, with the next edition in 2028. Beyond the museum, use its digital art map to discover sculptures, murals and other public artworks around the city – and see why Borås is known as ‘the sculpture city’.

Housed in a former power station with a striking orange-red extension, it’s just a 10-minute walk from Malmö Central Station. Beyond the exhibitions, there’s a varied programme for all ages, from baby painting and creative workshops to Drink & Draw sessions and peaceful mornings at the museum.

Britta Marakatt-Labba has gained international recognition for her extraordinary embroideries. Her drawings and watercolours, however, are almost entirely unknown – works she has kept out of the public eye until now. The exhibition at The Nordic Watercolour Museum focuses on Britta Marakatt-Labba’s works on paper, which are being shown publicly for the first time. The exhibition features around 140 works, primarily watercolours, drawings and sketches, complemented by a selection of embroideries and graphic works.

Opening hours:

At The Nordic Watercolour Museum, you can explore current exhibitions, engage in something creative, or take in the breathtaking views of the nearby archipelago on the Swedish West Coast. The museum is a place for all ages – whether you want to experience art, take part in activities, or simply enjoy a peaceful moment by the water. Discover what’s on and plan your visit.

- 27 Nov 3.00 PM–9.00 PM\\ \\ **Friday Evening at the Museum – full programme!**\\ \\ On Friday 27 November, we invite you to spend the evening at The Nordic Watercolour Museum! Enjoy late-night opening hours, guided tours of the exhibitions, live performances and a lively atmosphere at Vatten Restaurang & Kafé.

Over the past decade, Britta Marakatt-Labba has made an almost unparalleled breakthrough. Her embroidered narratives revolve around Sámi life in close relationship with nature, but also around colonialism, loss and resistance – about the face of racism, human greed and the lost lands once grazed by the animals. The drawings and watercolours, created largely without any intention of being exhibited publicly, are thematically closely related to her embroideries. Similar motifs recur in the works on paper, but in a new and more intimate form.

## This is The Nordic Watercolour Museum

Welcome to The Nordic Watercolour Museum – a vibrant meeting place for art, nature, and creativity by the sea. Here, you can experience contemporary watercolour art, be inspired by our unique setting, or take part in exciting activities for all ages. All year round.

- **School**\\ \\ Would you like to visit the museum with your SCHOOL? The Nordic Watercolour Museum is an inquisitive museum that believes in the connection between art and knowledge. We actively engage in educational work through exhibitions and workshops for all ages. A visit to the museum can take many forms. As a class, you can choose to explore the museum independently or accompanied by our art educators.

- **History and architecture**\\ \\ The Nordic Watercolour Museum has been welcoming visitors for 26 years, but the dream of a museum dedicated to watercolour techniques goes back even further. Our HISTORY of how this meeting place for creativity, culture, and nature came to be is filled with passionate individuals, bold visions, and visitor numbers that have exceeded all expectations.

Unlike many other museums, The Nordic Watercolour Museum does not have a permanent exhibition of works from its collection. Instead, we continuously showcase selections from it. By working solely with temporary exhibitions, we are able to present a larger portion of our collection over time. The collection is a living and vital part of the museum's activities, and you can discover more about it here on our website.

At The Nordic Watercolour Museum, you can view exhibitions from around the world, attend exciting events, experiment with colour and enjoy delicious dining. Come and experience encounters between nature, art and people.

Opening hours & admission Find us

The small coastal town of Skärhamn on the island of Tjörn is home to The Nordic Watercolour Museum. It attracts visitors from all continents – keen to experience contemporary art and the history of watercolour. The cultural offering makes this a vibrant location all year round and the museum is open throughout the seasons (except when closed for change-over of exhibitions). Thanks to its unique location right by the water’s edge, visitors to the museum can combine art experiences with a dip from the jetty. Welcome to The Nordic Watercolour Museum!

The Nordic Watercolour Museum is a place for all people and all ages. Bring the whole family and discover everything the museum has to offer. A number of our events are aimed at families and younger visitors, and these vary depending on the period. Perhaps you are interested in painting, guided tours or a performance? In addition, the museum has plenty of spots where you can sit for a while, to draw, read or discuss what you have seen. And why not refuel with some delicious cake in the café?

The museum shop stocks a carefully selected range of watercolour materials, literature, crafts and Nordic design items. The assortment varies, in keeping with the current exhibition and the season. There is always an exciting selection to browse, for both adults and children.

Both children and adults can try their hand at watercolour art in our open studio, with watercolour materials and staff on hand to offer help if needed. Themed workshops take place during school holidays, with extended opening hours and free admission. Keep an eye on our events page to check opening hours and current information.

- **Opening hours & admission**

When the museum is closed, you can enjoy some outdoor **art**. _The Lighthouse_ is a cylindrical sculpture six metres in height by artist duo Wolfgang Winter and Berthold Hörbelt. It sits on a rocky islet right beside The Nordic Watercolour Museum; at night, it is illuminated, and inside is a bench. Gunilla Hansson’s installation _Singing Inhabitants_ runs along the deck surrounding the museum. The inscribed text tells of an atoll in the Pacific Ocean that is at risk of being swamped by rising sea levels.

The museum is located next to **Gråskärsbadet**, one of Tjörn’s largest bathing areas. It has a sandy beach, a diving platform, a beach volleyball court and public toilets. Above the bathing area stands _Hulda_, a sculpture by artist Linn Granlund owned by Tjörn Municipality.

Tjörn is also home to **Sculpture in Pilane**: a sculpture park and eight-hectare cultural landscape. The exhibition area is not a traditional park but a living landscape with grazing sheep, where you can wander freely or follow well-trodden paths over meadows and rocky outcrops. The rocky summits afford outstanding views of the North Sea and the Bohuslän archipelago. A 12-km hiking and cycling trail runs between The Nordic Watercolour Museum and Pilane, through one of Sweden’s most scenic cultural landscapes. More information.

In southern Sweden, **Karlskrona’s naval port** showcases Sweden’s maritime legacy. Built in 1680, this UNESCO site was designed for constructing warships and remains a captivating destination for fans of naval and military history.

Nearby, visitors can dive into Swedish pop history at the **ABBA Museum**, or explore the life and legacy of global music icon Avicii at **The Avicii Experience**, part of the immersive SPACE digital culture centre. At **Tekniska museet** (the Swedish National Museum of Science and Technology), the new 360-degree **Wisdome** dome experience brings science to life in a big, bold way.

On the west coast, the island of Tjörn is home to **Pilane**, an open-air sculpture park set among ancient grazing lands – a unique combination of nature, art and history. Just a scenic cycle away is the **Nordic Watercolour Museum**, right by the water’s edge.

With a day pass for the **Stockholm metro**, your clients can explore 110 km of underground art. Each station features unique artworks – murals, mosaics, installations and sculptures – turning the daily commute into a cultural adventure. Highlights include **Kungsträdgården** station, where the design references local plant life and the former 17th-century palace, _Makalös_, that once stood nearby.

Stockholm Slides at Moderna Museet

Set on the island of Skeppsholmen in central Stockholm, Moderna Museet is one of Europe’s leading museums of modern and contemporary art. Its impressive collection of over 140,000 works includes paintings, sculptures, photography and film by artists such as Picasso and Dalí. Don’t miss Stockholm Slides, Carsten Höller’s playful artwork featuring two slides that whisk visitors from the museum’s rooftop to ground level (closed during the colder months). The building also houses ArkDes, Sweden’s national museum of architecture and design.

A waterfront dining experience at Fotografiska’s restaurant in Stockholm, combining seasonal cuisine with striking views and photography exhibitions.

Since opening in Stockholm in 2010, Fotografiska has expanded to cities including Berlin, Tallinn, Shanghai and Shenzhen. Located on Södermalm, this photography museum has no permanent collection, instead presenting changing exhibitions by established and emerging photographers from around the world. Open until late in the evening, it also hosts talks and events. Round off your visit at the award-winning restaurant, serving seasonal food with panoramic views across the water.

Just 30 minutes from central Stockholm, Artipelag brings together art, design, food and nature in a striking waterfront setting on Värmdö island. Its name combines ‘art’ and ‘archipelago’, reflecting its location in the Stockholm archipelago. The purpose-built museum hosts changing exhibitions, while large windows frame views of the surrounding forest and sea. Explore the outdoor sculpture park or enjoy a meal overlooking the water. On weekends, a direct bus connects Artipelag with central Stockholm.

Housed in a former boiler house beneath the Älvsborg Bridge in Gothenburg, Röda Sten Konsthall has a colourful past. Once a venue for rave parties and threatened with demolition, the industrial building is now a hub for contemporary art, showcasing sculpture, installations, photography and video art. The gallery also hosts talks and workshops and organises the Gothenburg International Biennial for Contemporary Art (GIBCA), held across the city. The next edition runs from 4 September to 21 November 2027.

With a focus on contemporary and public art, Borås Konstmuseum showcases Swedish and international artists through painting, sculpture, photography and moving images. Admission is free, and visitors can explore exhibitions, guided tours and creative activities. Since 2008, the museum has organised the Borås International Sculpture Biennial, with the next edition in 2028. Beyond the museum, use its digital art map to discover sculptures, murals and other public artworks around the city – and see why Borås is known as ‘the sculpture city’.

Opened in 2009 as a branch of Stockholm’s renowned Moderna Museet, the Malmö museum showcases modern and contemporary art by Swedish and international artists, drawing on the museum’s extensive collection alongside temporary exhibitions. Housed in a former power station with a striking orange-red extension, it’s just a 10-minute walk from Malmö Central Station. Beyond the exhibitions, there’s a varied programme for all ages, from baby painting and creative workshops to Drink & Draw sessions and peaceful mornings at the museum.

The crown jewel of Sweden’s art museums is the iconic Nationalmuseum in the capital of Stockholm. Since its establishment in 1866, it has served as a premier setting for masterworks in painting, sculpture, art and design dating from the 1500s to the 1900s.

In addition to the extensive permanent collection, Nationalmuseum features regular and temporary exhibitions with top artists from around the globe.

The Nationalmuseum is a landmark building overlooking the water with stunning views of the Royal Palace. The museum enjoys the best of classic architecture combined with modern convenience.
